tristan.note: Eliot’s notes cite the libretto by act and verse: I, verses 5–8, and III, verse 24. The young sailor’s song is the first thing sung in the opera; the sailor sings it unseen, from the masthead, above the deck where Isolde lies. The shepherd’s “Öd und leer das Meer!” comes in Act III, answering Tristan’s servant Kurwenal, who has asked whether any ship is in sight while Tristan lies wounded and waiting for Isolde. In the poem the hyacinth garden (lines 35–41) falls between the two quotations. Eliot heard Tristan, or its music in concert, in Boston in the autumn of 1909, at the start of his graduate year at Harvard, and wrote a poem about it, “Opera,” dated November 1909. Stravinsky, who met him in December 1956, wrote in “Memories of T. S. Eliot” (Esquire, August 1965) that Tristan “must have been one of the most passionate experiences of his life.” Ludwig II of Bavaria, whose money paid for the first performance, was found dead in 1886 in the Starnberger See, the lake of line 8.

baudelaire-au-lecteur.date: 1855; the preface poem of the 1857 volume
baudelaire-au-lecteur.note: Baudelaire opens his book by listing the sins of mankind, keeping the worst, boredom, for last, and then turning on whoever is reading. Eliot closes his first section the same way. In his essay “Baudelaire” (1930) he called him “the greatest exemplar in modern poetry in any language,” and in “What Dante Means to Me” (1950) he said he had learned from him “the possibility of fusion between the sordidly realistic and the phantasmagoric.”

death-of-st-narcissus.note: The poem was set in type for Poetry (Chicago) in 1915 and withdrawn in proof; it was first published in 1950. It is about a saint who believes he has been a tree, a fish and a young girl, and who dies pierced with arrows. Two manuscripts, a rough draft and a fair copy, survived among the papers Eliot sent in 1922 to John Quinn, the New York lawyer and collector, with the Waste Land drafts; they are now in the Berg Collection of the New York Public Library and are reproduced in the 1971 facsimile. After these two lines the speaker promises to show the listener something other than the listener’s own shadow, sprawling on the sand at daybreak or leaping behind the fire against a red rock. The Waste Land keeps the second line, with “gray” changed to “red,” and reshapes the first. The poem is still in copyright, so only its first two lines are given here.

huxley-crome-yellow.note: Huxley’s country-house satire was published in November 1921. Its Mr. Scogan, a cynical guest who dresses up as an old gypsy woman to tell fortunes at the charity fair in the park under the name “Sesostris, the Sorceress of Ecbatana,” is the source usually given for Madame Sosostris. Asked about it by the critic Grover Smith, Eliot wrote to him on 10 March 1952 that he was “almost certain” he had taken the name from Crome Yellow without being conscious of doing so. Lawrence Rainey (Revisiting The Waste Land, 2005) has doubted it: he dates the typescript of Parts I and II to May 1921 from its paper and typewriter, before Huxley had finished the novel, and suggests the name was Eliot’s own. Huxley and Eliot had known each other since the war years through Lady Ottoline Morrell’s circle at Garsington, her house near Oxford.

dante-inf3.note: Inside the gate (“Abandon all hope”) but before the river Acheron, Dante finds the souls who were neither good nor bad, “who lived without infamy and without praise.” Heaven has cast them out and Hell will not receive them; they run for ever after a banner, stung by wasps. Eliot’s note on line 63 quotes lines 55–57 as the source of the crowd flowing over London Bridge, and his note on line 46 says that the “crowds of people” in Madame Sosostris’s cards “appear later,” which has generally been taken to mean this crowd. Eliot said in “What Dante Means to Me” (1950) that Dante’s poetry was still, “after forty years,” “the most persistent and deepest influence” on his own verse.

dante-inf4.note: Limbo, the first circle of Hell, holds the virtuous who died unbaptised, Homer, Virgil and Aristotle among them; Dante calls them the “great spirits” (spiriti magni), and they are not tormented but live in desire without hope. Eliot’s note on line 64 cites these lines. The comparison likens the sighs of the crowd on London Bridge to those of Limbo, where there is grief but no torment, not to the cries of the damned.

chaucer.note: The Prologue opens with April rain ending the drought of March, sap rising, birds singing and people longing to go on pilgrimage. Eliot’s notes say nothing of Chaucer; readers have long set “April is the cruellest month” against these lines, in which the same month and the same rain are welcome. In Eliot’s poem it is winter that “kept us warm” (lines 5–6).

tennyson.note: Eliot’s notes cite neither poem. The mad speaker of Maud, who imagines himself buried under a city street with the traffic going over him, is the source usually given for “a handful of dust” (line 30), and the passage has been compared with the “rats’ alley” of Part II. The Prince’s song in The Princess, with Swinburne’s “Itylus” (“Swallow, my sister, O sister swallow”) beside it, is the source usually given for “O swallow swallow” at line 429, the English half of a line whose Latin half is from the Pervigilium Veneris. In his essay “In Memoriam” (1936) Eliot wrote that Tennyson “had the finest ear of any English poet since Milton.”

whitman-lilacs.note: Whitman’s elegy for Lincoln, who was shot in April 1865, brings together the lilac, the evening star and the hermit thrush singing in a swamp. Eliot’s poem opens with lilacs bred out of the dead land (line 2) and the hermit-thrush’s “water-dripping song” is at line 357; Eliot’s note on that line describes the bird and quotes Chapman’s Handbook of Birds of Eastern North America, and says nothing of Whitman. In 1928 Eliot wrote that he “did not read Whitman until much later in life, and had to conquer an aversion to his form, as well as to much of his matter, in order to do so.” Two years earlier, reviewing a life of Whitman, he had written that “when Whitman speaks of the lilacs or of the mocking-bird, his theories and beliefs drop away like a needless pretext” (“Whitman and Tennyson,” Nation and Athenaeum, 18 December 1926). The case that the poem drew on Whitman all the same is made at length in S. Musgrove’s T. S. Eliot and Walt Whitman (1952).

webster-white-devil.note: Webster’s tragedy is about Vittoria Corombona, the “white devil” of the title, and her lover Brachiano, who has her husband and his own wife murdered. Vittoria’s mother Cornelia sings the dirge over her son Marcello, killed by his brother Flamineo; Flamineo makes the speech about widows in the last scene, rising from a feigned death after Vittoria and her maid Zanche have fired at him pistols they took to be loaded. Eliot’s notes cite the dirge at line 74 and Flamineo’s speech at line 408. At line 74 the poem turns Webster’s wolf, “foe to men,” into a Dog, “friend to men.” Eliot’s “Whispers of Immortality” (1918) begins “Webster was much possessed by death / And saw the skull beneath the skin.”

shakespeare-tempest.note: Ferdinand, washed ashore after the shipwreck, believes his father Alonso drowned; the song Ariel sings to him, unseen, describes a drowned man turned to coral and pearl. The song is not true. Alonso is alive, and the play ends with father and son reunited; in the poem the Phoenician Sailor of line 47 and Phlebas in Part IV stay drowned. Eliot’s notes cite the scene at lines 192 and 257, and his note on the pearls of line 125 refers them back to lines 37 and 48. His note on Tiresias says the Phoenician Sailor “is not wholly distinct from Ferdinand Prince of Naples.” Ferdinand’s “the king my father’s wreck” becomes “the king my brother’s wreck” and “the king my father’s death” for the fisherman on the canal bank behind the gashouse (lines 191–192).

frazer.note: Frazer’s twelve-volume study of magic and religion, which Eliot’s headnote says “has influenced our generation profoundly,” argued that the myths of Adonis, Attis and Osiris tell one story, that of a god who dies with the harvest and returns with the spring, helped by rites in which a king is sacrificed or an effigy is buried or drowned, and that the Church’s Easter was adapted from the spring festivals of Adonis and Attis. The two volumes Eliot names describe the “gardens of Adonis,” pots of quick-sprouting seed carried out with images of the dead god and “flung with them into the sea,” and the effigies of Osiris “made of earth and corn” that the priests buried so that grain would sprout from the god’s body. Eliot’s note on the Tarot says the Hanged Man “is associated in my mind with the Hanged God of Frazer”; the corpse planted in Stetson’s garden (line 71) and Phlebas in the current (line 312) have been connected with the same rites. Frazer put a reproduction of Turner’s painting The Golden Bough (1834) at the front of his first edition and opened his first page with it, describing it as a view of Lake Nemi. It in fact shows Lake Avernus, with the Sibyl of Cumae, the prophetess of the poem’s epigraph, holding the bough that admits Aeneas to the underworld.

weston.note: Weston (1850–1928) was a scholar of Arthurian romance. Following Frazer’s Golden Bough, she argued that the Grail stories preserved the remains of an ancient fertility cult: a king whose wound lays his land waste, a cup and a lance that were sexual symbols before they were Christian relics, and a rite of initiation descended from the mystery cults of Attis and Mithra. Those cults, she says, were carried across the Roman Empire by Syrian merchants, slaves and soldiers (chapter XII). Medievalists have not accepted the argument. Eliot’s headnote says the book suggested “not only the title, but the plan and a good deal of the incidental symbolism of the poem,” and recommends it “to any who think such elucidation of the poem worth the trouble”; in a lecture of 1956 he said he regretted “having sent so many enquirers off on a wild goose chase after Tarot cards and the Holy Grail.” The chapters the poem draws on most are II (The Task of the Hero), VI (The Symbols, where the Grail hallows become the four suits of the Tarot), IX (The Fisher King) and XIII (The Perilous Chapel).

petronius.note: The speaker is Trimalchio, a freed slave grown enormously rich, boasting to his guests between courses; his dinner party is the longest continuous episode in what survives of the Satyricon. The Sibyl of Cumae, in Ovid’s telling (Metamorphoses XIV), asked Apollo for as many years as there were grains in a heap of dust she had scooped up, and forgot to ask for youth to go with them; she foresees that she will shrink until only her voice is left. The typescript of the poem carried a different epigraph, from Conrad’s Heart of Darkness, ending “The horror! the horror!”; Pound doubted that Conrad was weighty enough for the place, and Eliot put Petronius in its place before publication.

dante-purg26.note: On the seventh terrace of Purgatory, where the lustful walk in flame, Dante meets the poet Guido Guinizelli, who points out the troubadour Arnaut Daniel as “miglior fabbro del parlar materno,” the better craftsman of the mother tongue (line 117). Arnaut answers in his own Provençal, the only passage in the Comedy in a vernacular other than Italian, and steps back into the fire. Eliot took the title of his 1920 collection Ara Vos Prec from line 145 (the Ovid Press title page misprinted it “Ara Vus Prec,” a form Eliot later blamed on his Italian edition of Dante), and line 428 of the poem from line 148, which his note quotes with the three lines before it. The dedication “For Ezra Pound / il miglior fabbro” was not printed in 1922: Eliot wrote it into Pound’s copy of the Boni & Liveright edition in January 1923, and it first appeared in print in Poems 1909–1925. The phrase was already Pound’s own: “Il Miglior Fabbro” is the title of his chapter on Arnaut Daniel in The Spirit of Romance (1910). Modern texts read “li affina”; Eliot’s “gli” follows the older text he used.

dickens-omf.note: Betty Higden, a poor old woman who minds children for a living, is praising Sloppy, a foundling brought up in the workhouse who lives with her and turns her mangle, and who reads her the newspaper and does all the voices in the police-court reports. “He Do the Police in Different Voices” is typed as a title at the head of the typescripts of Parts I and II in the drafts; it did not survive to publication. The novel opens on the Thames, with Gaffer Hexam and his daughter in a boat searching the water for drowned bodies.

conrad-hod.note: Kurtz’s last words stood on the title page of the typescript, as the poem’s epigraph. Kurtz is the trader whom the narrator, Marlow, has gone up the river to find. Pound, returning the poem in January 1922, wrote that he doubted whether Conrad was “weighty enough to stand the citation.” Eliot answered that it was “much the most appropriate I can find, and somewhat elucidative,” and Pound withdrew the objection (the exchange is printed in the 1971 facsimile and in the Letters, volume 1); Eliot nevertheless replaced it with the passage from Petronius that stands there now. “The heart of light” at line 41 has been read as an inversion of Conrad’s title. The story is told on a yawl at anchor in the Thames estuary at dusk, with London upriver.

eliot-frontiers.note: Eliot gave the lecture at the University of Minnesota on 30 April 1956, to an audience of about fourteen thousand; it was printed in On Poetry and Poets (1957). Thirty-four years on, Eliot said he had meant only to list his references, “spiking the guns” of critics who had accused his earlier poems of plagiarism. The poem’s first printings, in two magazines, the Criterion and the Dial, had no notes; when Boni & Liveright were to make it a book, it was found too short, and he expanded the notes to fill the pages, with the result he called “bogus scholarship.” He regretted sending readers on “a wild goose chase after Tarot cards and the Holy Grail,” and said the notes could not now be removed, since anyone who bought his poems and found them missing would ask for his money back.
